stories.title: Nobel Peace Prize winner Pillay surprised by honour
stories.summary: The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 has been awarded to Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said. "This year's laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted," said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo. Ms Pillay joked that she might "share the prize" with US President Donald Trump if people kept applauding. "If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she said in a video posted to X by Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard, which showed Ms Pillay being applauded after the announcement of the award. stories.title: Missed cancer diagnosis apology 'too little, too late'
stories.summary: University Hospital Galway has apologised to a woman who was diagnosed with terminal brain cancer in 2023 after a number of scans were misinterpreted. Mary Keane, from Co Mayo, said that doctors paid "no heed" to her and described the apology as "too little, too late". She had been attending neurologists at UHG with headaches dating back to 2009. Ms Keane was reassured that they were connected to bruising from an old head injury from an event which happened in 2005. However, she continued to suffer chronic headaches to the extent that she could not work. Despite multiple attendances to the hospital's Neurology Department she was primarily treated with painkillers.

stories.title: SF, People Before Profit representatives get PSNI letters
stories.summary: Sinn Féin and People Before Profit elected representatives in Northern Ireland have received letters from police probing alleged criminal offences in the ongoing parading dispute in Portadown. In a statement, Sinn Féin said a number of representatives and party members have received correspondence from police in relation to protests on the Garvaghy Road. It said the party "stood with the residents of the Garvaghy Road for the last two weeks in the face of provocation and the threat of an unwanted Orange march through their community". Earlier, People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll said he has been invited to attend a voluntary interview under caution in connection with protests on the Garvaghy Road. In a statement, he said he will be seeking the advice of his solicitor, adding: "Standing up for what's right is never wrong." The Police Service of Northern Ireland said individuals "reasonably suspected of committing offences" would receive letters for interview.

stories.title: DCC Energy to sell tech unit Nexora for $725m
stories.summary: Energy distributor DCC Energy said today it would sell its technology division, Nexora, to private equity firm One Equity Partners for a total enterprise value of $725m on a cash- and debt-free basis. The sale of the business is expected to complete on or after March 1, 2027, subject to regulatory approvals, DCC said in a statement. DCC agreed to a £5.75 billion takeover by a consortium of US private equity firms KKR and Energy Capital Partners in July. DCC said its shareholders will receive an additional 42 pence per share on top of the existing offer from the KKR-led consortium. But if regulatory conditions related to the sale of Nexora are not met by July 31, 2027, the additional consideration will be zero, it added. Donal Murphy, the chief executive of DCC Energy, said Nexora has been an important part of the DCC Group for many years and has built a strong market position through the expertise and commitment of its people.

stories.title: Russian bomb kills 33 in street in east Ukraine city
stories.summary: Ukraine accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians after more than 30 people were killed when two buses were blown up in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, in one of the deadliest attacks in weeks. President Volodymyr Zelensky vowed that it "will not go unanswered" after photos posted by local authorities showed the burnt-out metal shell of the vehicles, with bodies and debris strewn across the road. "Russia is trying to destroy all life in (the) Donbas (region) and the world must respond to this," he wrote on Telegram, warning the death toll could rise. Kramatorsk City Council called it "yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population," adding there were "absolutely no military targets" in the area. "The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians," Donetsk governor Vadym Filashkin said, accusing Moscow of flouting "every conceivable rule of warfare and norm of international humanitarian law". Three more people were killed in shelling at a nearby village, the emergency services said.

stories.title: Wafer misses out as Bemand names squad for South Africa
stories.summary: Ireland head coach Scott Bemand has named a 30-player squad that will face South Africa in back-to-back WXV Global Series Tests on 24 October and 31 October - with Aoife Wafer and Sam Monahan. Wafer has been dealing with an ankle injury while Monahan suffered a knee injury while on duty for Gloucester-Hartpury in August. The games, coming after their home loss to USA and victories over Japan, will be played at the Athlone Stadium in Cape Town. Erin King will lead the 30-player travelling squad, with recently capped players Beth Buttimer, Jemima Adams Verling, Kate Jordan, Sophie Barrett and Alana McInerney all included. Second row Ruth Campbell returns from injury to travel with the squad but Monaghan and Wafer have been ruled out. After a remote training week following their recent victories over Japan in Galway and Cork, Ireland return to camp at the IRFU High Performance Centre on Monday before travelling to Cape Town on Thursday.

stories.title: Underdogs could get home advantage in new Leinster format
stories.summary: Leinster GAA chairperson Martin Byrne says the province will be open to the prospect of giving underdogs home advantage in knockout games under the council's proposed new championship structure. A motion to Congress 2027 is being drafted following Leinster GAA management approval with a view to forming an eight-team provincial SHC, which would be split into two groups of four. In that instance, Group 1 would comprise higher tier teams made up of the top four teams from the 2027 series. Group 2 would feature the fifth and sixth-placed teams from ’27, along with the two Joe McDonagh Cup finalists. Byrne revealed his council will remain open to the possibility of an underdog receiving home advantage in a knockout game. "Where venues come up in all of this will be decided by our CCCC (Central Competitions Control Committee) in 2028," he said.

stories.title: URC teams: Provinces welcome back internationals for R3
stories.summary: The Irish provinces have welcomed back a host of their international frontline stars, ahead of this weekend's Round 3 games in the BKT United Rugby Championship. Ulster and Munster's Interpro in Belfast is the marquee game of the weekend on Saturday night, with Tadhg Beirne back in to captain Munster at Affidea Stadium, while Ulster head coach Richie Murphy has been able to recall Nick Timoney, Stuart McCloskey, Jacob Stockdale and Rob Baloucoune for their first games of the season. It's the same front row that started against Glasgow, with Eric O’Sullivan, Tom Stewart and former Munster man Keynan Knox packing down, with Ben Donnell joining Eli Snyman in the second row. Cormac Izuchukwu shifts to flanker, with Timoney and Juarno Augustus both coming in to form a new back row, replacing James McKillop, David McCann and the injured Bryn Ward. Nathan Doak starts his first game of the season at scrum-half, and Matthew Devine is named on the bench, having been an injury concern this week. Jack Murphy continues in the 10 shirt, with McCloskey coming in for Ben Carson at centre, and Jamie Benson pivoting to the 13 shirt.

stories.title: Dream big - inside The Ark's new anthology of plays for kids
stories.summary: Aideen Howard, creative director of The Ark, introduces Dream Big, the new book collecting a quintet of original (and acclaimed) theatre works commissioned by the children's cultural centre. As a young drama student in 1995, I remember vividly the excitement surrounding the opening of Europe's first ever dedicated children cultural centre. That this ground-breaking innovation was happening in the heart of Dublin city was a source of pride. The Ark Children’s Cultural Centre opened its doors in Temple Bar, three years after the Irish government ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of The Child which recognised the right of children to 'participate freely in cultural life and the arts.’ History was being made. Ireland was showing a new cultural confidence in its vision for investment in both the arts and children. Now, thirty years after its founding, over a million children and their parents and teachers have attended The Ark. Our purpose is to realise children’s right to art and culture with ambition and joy. We do so by commissioning, producing and presenting new art for, by, with and about children from birth to age 12. From the beginning I was inspired by The Ark’s radical approach to art making and community engagement. When I was appointed Director in 2015, I was keen to build on those strong foundations. One of my first projects was to introduce a child participation practice to redistribute decision making power across the organisation alongside a new commissioning strategy. The Ark Children’s Council was established and now plays a key role in all decision-making and inform the development of every new commission. The five writers featured in Dream Big have created new worlds of the imagination.

stories.title: Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour gets new opening acts
stories.summary: Former The Fray star Isaac Slade and American Idol contestant Brooks Rosser have joined Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour. Sheeran lost his opening acts after US rapper Macklemore was dropped from the tour over comments he made about Gaza. Shortly after, Sheeran’s other supporting acts, including Irish singer Aaron Rowe, musician Finneas, who is Billie Eilish’s brother, and Danish singer Lukas Graham, as well as his backing band Beoga, dropped out of the remaining dates. Slade, who was previously the lead singer of rock band The Fray, has joined the tour as a support act for Sheeran’s dates in Indianapolis on 10 October, Charlotte on 17 October, Arlington on 24 October and Tampa on 7 November. Slade shared the dates on his Instagram and wrote: "See you out there." Rosser, who was a contestant on season 24 of American Idol, will also perform on the 10 October date in Indianapolis.

stories.title: Irish designer Sasha Donnellan on finding her calling in Paris
stories.summary: Ellen Corcoran meets with Sasha Donnellan, the Irish designer who has captivated celebrity clients like Laura Whitmore and Roz Purcell, ahead of a dazzling presentation of her work during Paris Fashion Week. In the foyer of Hôtel Le Marois, I meet an elated and energetic Sasha Donnellan. She has a suitcase full of garments to bring back to Ireland ahead of her Ireland Fashion Week show in Dublin on Sunday morning, where she will showcase her full 20-look collection. The crowd finally fizzles out of the building and we find a seat by a grand piano as she catches her breath. Just 15 minutes earlier, a glimpse of her brand new collection, 'The Calling', had graced the runway for the very first time as part of Flying Solo NYC’s Paris Fashion Week show. Naturally, I ask how she’s feeling. "I was very nervous, of course, but also excited to see how people would perceive it, because I think this collection is quite different to my previous work", she says. "I feel like previous collections were much more focused on silks, and this time, I really leaned into my outerwear interest. That's something I haven't done before. So I was excited to see how people would react." Sasha refers to each of her collections as "little chapters" of her life. "I’m a designer, I love storytelling. To me, each collection represents a chapter that reflects something I'm incredibly passionate about at that moment." This time, that meant exploring the idea of a calling. Following her hugely successful Ireland Fashion Week debut in 2025, Sasha made the decision to become independent and commit fully to working on her brand, a move that prompted her to think about the people throughout history who had followed their own sense of purpose.

stories.summary: The meeting came a day after Mr O'Donovan said the broadcaster would receive €240m for 2027, which was €20m less than the €260m envisaged. Speaking after the meeting, Mr Bakhurst said he had "an extremely constructive meeting with the minister". He explained how he had agreed to "carry on working with his officials to try to find a resolution to this but it was very positive, which was very welcome for our part". In a statement, the Department of Communications described the meeting as "positive".

stories.title: Polls close in London by-election to replace Starmer
stories.summary: Polls have closed in a by-election to replace former Labour Party leader and British prime minister Keir Starmer as Holborn and St Pancras MP, with results expected to be announced in the early hours of tomorrow morning. The north London seat has been a Labour stronghold since its formation in 1983, held by Frank Dobson for 32 years and Mr Starmer for 11. However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski is hoping to break Labour's clean sheet and secure his own seat in the House of Commons. The by-election comes in a difficult week for Mr Polanski’s party, after a controversial motion was passed at the Green Party conference asserting that "Zionism is racism". Mr Polanski, who abstained on the vote, later said that he will "not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of". Labour’s candidate in the by-election is Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, who is the bookies’ favourite to win.

stories.title: 28% of new private cars licensed so far this year EVs
stories.summary: New figures from the Central Statistics Office show that new private electric cars licensed for the first time in September grew by 54% on the same time last year. The CSO said that 3,074 new private electric cars were licensed in September compared with 2,000 for the same month in 2025. Today's figures show that licensing of hybrid vehicles decreased by 2% from 1,217 in September last year to 1,197 new private cars in September of this year. But the number of new plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) licensed grew by 24% with 1,296 such vehicles licensed last month compared to 1,045 the same time last year. The CSO said the share of electric vehicles among new private cars from January to September rose to 28% compared with 19% for the same time in 2025. It added that the combined share of petrol and diesel cars among new private cars licensed so far this year fell to 31% from 43% in 2025.

stories.title: Search warrants for ex-prince Andrew's homes 'unlawful'
stories.summary: A criminal investigation into former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing despite the search warrants that allowed British police officers to raid two of his properties being ruled unlawful, the High Court in London has heard. The former Duke of York had launched a legal challenge against Thames Valley Police over the lawfulness of the warrants issued by a judge at the Old Bailey allowing officers to raid his residence on the Sandringham Estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, in February. At a hearing at the Royal Courts of Justice today, which Andrew did not attend, Mr Justice Hilliard said that "agreement was reached between the claimant and Thames Valley Police that the search warrants were unlawful". But the judge also said that "the fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring an investigation to an end, or mean that the whole of the investigation was unlawful". And a Thames Valley Police spokesperson said in a statement after the hearing that "the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed. "Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation.

stories.title: Cullen excited by return to Leinster's 'quirky' home
stories.summary: It feels like an age since Leinster last hosted a competitive game at the RDS, a URC quarter-final against Connacht in late May, 2024. Just over 26 months and a €52m redevelopment later, Leo Cullen's side will finally get to run out at what is now called the Laya Arena, which is expected to come close to hitting its 20,500 capacity for its full opening against Cardiff on Saturday. They didn't have to move far during their two seasons away. In fact, they didn't even have to leave Ballsbridge, as they set up shop at Aviva Stadium, occasionally venturing to Croke Park. The Aviva is a great place to play, but it's not home. And as they prepare for their first home game of the new season, the Leinster head coach is excited about getting back to their new and improved - but still "quirky" venue. "It's an insane amount of rugby clubs in a very small area, and then we're playing in the showjumping arena, playing rugby. "So it's an amazing thing, because obviously my mum breeds horses and ponies, as some of you may well be aware of. So I've been going there since I was literally a baby.

stories.title: Mayo great Cillian O'Connor announces retirement
stories.summary: Mayo great Cillian O'Connor has announced his retirement from inter-county football at the age of 34 in the wake of the county's All-Ireland winning campaign. O'Connor, a two-time All-Star, who became the leading scorer in the history of the All-Ireland football championship in 2019, made the announcement in an extensive interview with the Irish Examiner's Maurice Brosnan. The Ballintubber forward confirmed he would not be part of the Mayo squad for the 2027 campaign. O'Connor had been a mainstay in the Mayo attack for over a decade, first breaking through as a regular starter as a 19-year old during James Horan's first year in charge. He was their primary marksman and top scorer for the remainder of the decade, during which Mayo reached four All-Ireland finals, suffering a series of agonising defeats, first to Donegal in 2012 and then to Dublin in 2013, 2016 and 2017. O'Connor surpassed Colm Cooper's all-time championship scoring record in the 2019 season and during the behind-closed-doors 2020 season, he posted another record as he racked up 4-09 in the All-Ireland semi-final victory over Tipperary, the highest ever tally registered by an individual in the championship game.

stories.summary: Shamrock Rovers welcome Drogheda United to Tallaght Stadium tonight aiming to reclaim top spot in what is developing into a thrilling SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division title race. The defending champions are chasing their sixth league crown in seven years but currently sit third in the table, albeit with only goal difference separating them, Bohemians and leaders St Patrick's Athletic. The Hoops would have been grateful for the international break coming when it did, as it gave manager Stephen Bradly a chance to reset following a dip in form from his side. A 3-2 victory over Waterford in their final game before the break was welcome but that was only their second league win since the end of July as Rovers appeared to be suffering from a major European hangover. The good news for Bradley and his side is that the league title is still very much within their grasp and a win over Drogheda would take them three points clear of the chasing pack, with the contenders all having played 32 games. With Rovers taking on Bohemians on Monday, a win for the Hoops is essential in what looks like being a pivotal few days in the title race.

stories.title: Open House Dublin - the festival of architecture returns
stories.summary: Emmett Scanlon, Director of the Irish Architecture Foundation, introduces the 2026 edition of Open House Dublin, the capital's festival of architecture, which returns this October. This year's Open House Festival explores the idea that "Dublin Is Living" and that people are its life support. On a daily basis, it is communities of place and interest, on streets, in rooms, parks and pitches, that form and shape Dublin city and county. This year we place this unique relationship between people and place front and centre at Ireland’s largest and longest running festival of architecture. Our nine-day festival invites you to explore the city and county and join a conversation about our capital's future. More than 200 free events are taking place, from behind-the-scenes tours to talks, workshops and exhibitions. People of all ages, backgrounds and abilities can discover Dublin and consider what it means to live, thrive and belong here. For younger visitors, Open House Junior brings architecture to life on 10–11 October with free workshops, walking tours and creative activities for children, teenagers and families to explore and reimagine the places around them. For the first time, our 'Open Table' series will take place across all four Dublin local authority areas. Hosted by housing and urban design expert Dr Lorcan Sirr, these lunchtime conversations are a chance to share experiences, local knowledge and ideas for their neighbourhoods. From 12-15 October, in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown, Fingal, South Dublin and Dublin City, the discussions will feed into the Dublin Is Living Town Hall. Happening on the evening of Thursday 15 October at Wood Quay, the Dublin Is Living Town Hall will bring together residents, community advocates, local business owners and voices from architecture and public life to discuss the big questions facing Dublin, including housing, vacant buildings, transport, green space, safety and belonging. Perspectives gathered at the Open Tables will bring neighbourhood experiences into this wider discussion about Dublin’s future.

stories.title: Why Irish designers are so drawn to the Gothic in fashion
stories.summary: Laura Fitzachary is a historian and historical content creator based in Dublin who specialises in fashion and beauty history in Ireland and beyond. Ahead of spooky season, fashion historian Laura Fitzachary explores how Gothic tropes and traditional Irish stories have Irish fashion designers enthralled. Inspired by storytelling and craftsmanship, Gothic fashion naturally finds a home in Ireland. So it is not surprising that Irish designers such as Jonathan Anderson, Dior Creative Director, and Simone Rocha have referenced Gothic literature, Irish mythology and Victorian mourning dress. A literal take on the iconic Dior Book Tote was revealed by Magherafelt-born Anderson in 2025 in the lead up Dior Homme SS '26, one of which featured an homage to the first edition of Dracula by Bram Stoker. As noted by Dior, Stoker’s Dracula take its place in Anderson’s "dream library". The Gothic horror novel was published in 1897 and draws extensively from folklore and history. While there are several theories as to who the character of 'Dracula’ is based on, this mystery has even spilled over into fashion. Alexander McQueen’s FW ‘09 Menswear featured models bearing a cane, a top hat and a coat draped over the shoulders – a direct nod to the human form of the vampire depicted by Gary Oldman in Bram Stoker’s Dracula, Francis Ford Coppola's 1992 interpretation of the novel. What is known is the strong influence of traditional Irish tales on Stoker’s writing, which has been argued by historians such as David J. Skal.

stories.title: US to livestream execution of Fort Hood mass shooter
stories.summary: The US will livestream the army's upcoming firing squad execution of a man who ⁠killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon has said, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution. Nidal Hasan, a former US army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945. The execution is scheduled for 3 December at the same Texas base where Hasan opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility. It comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the failed execution by injection of a Tennessee woman last week. "It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," a Pentagon official told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, confirmed plans to livestream the execution in an X post.

stories.title: Annual inflation at highest level since January 2024
stories.summary: A considerable jump in the cost of energy drove consumer prices 4.1% higher in the year to September, according to latest figures from the Central Statistics Office (CSO). The September annual increase compared with a 3.7% rise in the 12 months to August, and was the highest rate of inflation since January 2024. The CSO figures show that energy products - which includes electricity, gas and other fuels - were up by 15.3% in the year to September. These increases follow a jump in the cost of oil as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. Since March the cost to households for electricity, gas, and home-heating oil has risen significantly. A jump in mortgage interest rates of over 10% has also also contributed to higher consumer prices. Costs across education (+8.9%) and transport (+7.5%) have also added to higher prices.

stories.title: Govt 'tried to get balance' in budget spending - McEntee
stories.summary: Senior Government figures have defended the spending plans announced in Budget 2027, despite sharp criticism from the State's financial watchdog and opposition politicians. The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (IFAC) accused the coalition of playing "fast and loose" with the public finances, putting them on a worse trajectory. "The Government should be saving more, making its tax base more secure, and avoiding aimless drift" IFAC added in a statement. Minster for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee responded, saying: "There's people saying we spent too much, people saying not enough". She told reporters in Dublin that the Government had "tried to get a balance". The coalition has "invested in people and services", Ms McEntee said, including Income Tax changes, Carbon Tax policies and new plans to help people retrofit their homes.

stories.title: Are you due a tax refund? 3 tax credits you may not know about
stories.summary: Analysis: Thousands of taxpayers are missing out on refunds by not availing of tax credits for medical expenses, rent and college tuition fees. This article is now available as a Brainstorm podcast and can be heard above. You can also subscribe to the Brainstorm podcast through Apple Podcasts, Stitcher, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. While Benjamin Franklin once famously wrote "in this world nothing can be said to be certain except death and taxes", certainty is not the only thing these two have in common. Among other things, the tax world possesses its own reaper-like character, often manifesting in the shape of the dreaded "Tax Man". The prospect of having to engage with this looming spectre can create an understandable anxiety in the collective consciousness, an anxiety that is often exacerbated by the tax system itself. In Ireland most employees (whose only income source is their salary) manage to avoid ever having to engage directly with the Tax Man, namely the Revenue Commissioners. Our income tax bills are calculated and collected by our employers through payroll and passed directly to Revenue. In the past, we would have received a physical payslip, leading us to scratch our heads as to what the various figures meant. In these digital times, we seldom see any tax calculation detail, making the thoughts of engaging with Revenue even more anxiety-inducing. Fearful of the possibility of owing even more tax, we often leave well enough alone lest any contact with Revenue cost us more money. But there may well be a financial downside to this lack of engagement with Revenue. While most employers will have enough information to allocate the correct personal tax credits to their employees, some tax credits are dependent on payments made by the taxpayer themselves. As these won’t be reflected in payroll calculations, taxpayers must apply for these extra credits, or risk leaving money behind in the form of potential tax refunds. Here are three of the most underutilised tax credits.

stories.title: Thousands march in Madrid to honour pensioner Abascal
stories.summary: Thousands of Spaniards marched through central Madrid to mark the death of the 87-year-old woman whose ⁠eviction from her home ignited protests across the country and led to a snap election next month. Maricarmen Abascal, who died yesterday, had been hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her eviction on 23 September. No cause of death has been announced. Protests over home shortages and surging rents following her eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election for 29 November after parliament rejected his government's proposals to address a mounting housing crisis. As the sun set in Madrid, thousands followed a line of Tenants Union members, dressed in orange vests and walking arm-in-arm, as they carried a wreath of flowers from a protest camp in central Puerta del Sol square to Ms Abascal's former home near Retiro Park. "They're not deaths; they're murders," the protesters chanted. Several people who received eviction orders have died by suicide in Spain in recent months.

stories.title: Maresca: Manchester City achievements not tainted
stories.summary: Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca rejected suggestions the club's achievements have been tainted after they were found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules. An independent commission concluded more than £830million (€980m) of owner funding was used to inflate revenues and enable City to comply with Premier League and UEFA regulations through a series of "sham" arrangements between 2009 to 2018. However, City have lodged an appeal after stating the commission’s judgment contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe" and that there was "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence" to support their position. In his first press conference since the news broke Maresca, flanked by City’s chief communications officer Simon Heggie rather than the regular member of staff for such occasions, was asked whether the trophies won during the period in question were tainted. "Absolutely not. I know the effort from the players, the club and the manager at the time, Pep (Guardiola), so I don’t have any doubt about that," he said. "I understand the reason why most of you are here but the only thing I can say it is something I already said. There is a process ongoing and in this moment I completely trust the club. This is what I can say about that.
